batch.title: Water harvesting: findings that move a rating (first check)
batch.notes: Every water harvesting finding that no person has checked yet and that would change a rating if it were wrong. Each card says what the paper says, what we recorded and what looks wrong (or that it checks out), and what Approve or Reject would change today (trial run, 10 Nov). The AI's suggested call shows under the buttons; it is a suggestion only. Approve = recorded correctly, stays in use. Hold = leave it open with a note. Reject = set aside (kept on record, no longer counted); pick a reason.

relationship.outcome_raw: total nitrogen lost in run-off/sediment, graded soil bunds vs without (loss reduced)

context.note: review and synthesis of >100 Ethiopian SWC studies; pooled unweighted means per practice (Tables 2, 4-8)

units.question: Adimassu 2016 says graded soil bunds cut losses of soil nitrogen by up to 48% (organic matter 52%, phosphorus 41%). We recorded a strong water-cleaning benefit. Two doubts: 48% is the best case ('up to'), not the typical effect; and it is nutrients kept on the field, not water being cleaned. Approve keeps it. Reject: the one-paper water quality row for in-field practices ('strong positive') disappears; the separate low-income, upper-middle-income and semi-arid water quality lines would no longer show, as they would then match the overall rating. AI's view: A best-case figure is scored as strong, and soil nutrients kept on the field stand in for water quality.

relationship.outcome_raw: erosion accelerated by poorly maintained banquettes

context.note: national evaluation survey of 40 years of DRS (banquettes = contour bench terraces/ditches, 387 833 ha)

units.question: Arabi 2004 says badly maintained bench terraces end up speeding up erosion when breaches go unrepaired. We recorded erosion going up (a harm), which matches the quote. It is a maintenance failure, not the practice working as designed. Approve keeps this harm finding. Reject: erosion for the dryland Middle East and North Africa moves from 'conflicting evidence' to 'slight positive', with confidence from very low to low. AI's view: Direction is right on erosion; the maintenance condition is a real risk worth keeping.

units.citation: Brito, L.T. de L.; Moura, M.S.B. de; Gama, G.F.B. (eds. técnicos) (2007). Potencialidades da água de chuva no Semi-Árido brasileiro. Petrolina: Embrapa Semi-Árido. 181 p. ISBN 978-85-7405-009-6.
units.quote: tre estas tecnologias, o uso da irrigação de salvação tem reduzido os riscos da exploração agrícola em anos cuja precipitação pluviométrica é irregular, proporcionando até duas colheitas em anos considerados normais de chuvas. Segundo Porto et al. (1983), no Semi-Árido brasi- leiro, três em cada dez anos são considerados normais com relação à quantidade e à distribuição das chuvas. Define-se a irrigação de salvação como a lâmina de água aplicada à cul- tura nos veranicos que comumente ocorrem durante o período chuvoso na região Nordeste, de forma a não permitir que a cultura sofra estresse hídrico e, em alguns casos, morra. No Semi-Árido brasileiro, após as pri- meiras chuvas, é comum ocorrerem períodos de 20 a 30 dias sem novas chuvas, comprometendo seriamente a germinação e outras fases de de- senvolvimento das culturas. (English: [Am]ong these technologies, supplemental (salvation) irrigation has reduced the risks of farming in years with irregular rainfall, allowing up to two harvests in years considered normal. According to Porto et al. (1983), in the Brazilian semi-arid three in every ten years are considered normal in rainfall quantity and distribution. Salvation irrigation is defined as the depth of water applied to the crop during the dry spells (veranicos) that commonly occur during the rainy season in the Northeast, so as not to let the crop suffer water stress and, in some cases, die. In the Brazilian semi-arid, after the first rains, periods of 20 to 30 days without new rain are common, seriously compromising germination and other crop development phases.)

The probability of drought is 0.1 and cannot be mitigated since there is insuﬃcient
amount of water available for harvesting and hence for SI. Seventy-ﬁve per cent of
the severe dry spells can be partly mitigated with SI, but not fully as they occur late

the dry spell is only partly mitigated, transforming the severe dry spell to mild dry

units.quote:
Contrary to the expectations of this study, Log rank tests showed no significant 
differences for survival of the three-tree species in the three treatments (Table 4.12).

relationship.outcome_raw: survival over the trial of agroforestry tree seedlings planted in micro basins and trenches vs the ordinary planting hole (survival analysis, three species)

context.practice_as_described: Micro-catchments dug around newly planted agroforestry tree seedlings on farmers' homestead plots: (a) a micro basin (circular planting basin, stated radius 60 cm and depth 28 cm) and (b) a trench (stated length 160 cm, width 40 cm, depth 49.9 cm), both collecting rainfall runoff at the seedling. Seedlings of Cordia africana, Grevillea robusta and mango (Mangifera indica) planted in the main rainy season (June-September) and followed for 36 months (June 2013 - June 2016) on 29 farms (replicates). BASELINE (comparator): the ordinary planting hole dug to each farmer's own specification (control), same farm, same species.
context.note: Table 4.12 'Overall comparisons of tree survival in micro basin trench and control' (p72, thesis p60): Log Rank (Mantel-Cox), Breslow and Tarone-Ware tests per species and pooled, all P > 0.2 (pooled Log Rank P = 0.642). Thesis p73 (p61): 'the micro catchments did not significantly influence survival of either of the tree species'. Descriptive survival (Figures 4.6-4.8, pp69-71): Cordia africana survived better in the control than in either micro-catchment (six months: control 82%, micro basin and trench 64%); Grevillea robusta survived best in the micro basin by 18 months; mango best in the micro basin at 36 months - no consistent ordering. Small trial (at least three seedlings per treatment per farmer, 29 farmers). Mechanism intended: the basin / trench holds runoff at the seedling to extend soil moisture into the dry season; the author attributes the null to severe dry-season moisture scarcity that the structures could not bridge (farmers could not water: taps far from homes), plus insect/termite attack and free-grazing livestock browsing (pp73-75). Most deaths occurred 6-12 months after planting (onset of the dry season). Ordinary dry season, no named drought: no hazard_type. Design recorded as rct (on-farm replicated controlled trial; farmers volunteered, treatments not stated as randomised). Species pooled for the overall test, so claim_scope stays practice_technology.

units.quote:
Nyssen
(2001) studied the effects of stone bunds and grass strips
on soil loss reduction in Tigray at two experimental sites
using erosion plots. Reductions in soil loss of 61% and
64% due to stone bunds and of 25% and 62% due to grass
strips were measured.

Grass strips (25% and 62%) are vegetative, not water harvesting - not extracted.

Impactos de las zanjas de infiltración en el agua y los suelos: ¿Qué sabemos? Resumen de investigación. Lima: Forest Trends / Proyecto Infraestructura Natural para la Seguridad Hídrica (INSH).
units.quote: Entre los once estudios que midieron la escorrentía en 52 parcelas, todos mostraron una reducción en la escorrentía como resultado de las zanjas de infiltración. El análisis estadístico mostró que las zanjas de infiltración reducen significativamente la escorrentía. En promedio en los estudios anali- zados, las zanjas de infiltración redujeron la escorrentía en un 46.4%. En valores relativos esta reducción representa el 5.7% de la lluvia en promedio. (English: Among the eleven studies that measured runoff on 52 plots, all showed a reduction in runoff as a result of infiltration trenches. The statistical analysis showed that infiltration trenches significantly reduce runoff. On average in the studies analysed, infiltration trenches reduced runoff by 46.4%. In relative values this reduction represents 5.7% of rainfall on average.)

relationship.outcome_raw: plot-level runoff, infiltration trenches vs no trenches (meta-analysis)

context.note: Plot-scale meta-analysis by the review authors. The source files this result under its 'Reducción de la escorrentía e inundaciones' (peak-flow / flood) ecosystem service (Table 1, p.6); hazard_type=flood per that framing, but all pooled studies were plot-level. Infiltration trenches assigned to water_harvesting__in_situ (contour structures holding rain on the slope where it falls; no separate cropped receiving basin).

units.question: Locatelli 2020 (Spanish-language review) pooled 11 studies and found infiltration trenches cut runoff by 46.4% on average, a clear result. We recorded a strong runoff cut, and it feeds flood protection, as the review itself frames it. But these are small plots, not downstream floods. Approve keeps it. Reject: flood protection for water harvesting overall drops from moderate to 'conflicting evidence'; for in-field water capture it drops from high to no rating. AI's view: A pooled analysis with the number in the quote; the plot-to-flood step is the source's own framing.

units.quote:
The machine can construct bunds to cover about 3 ha 
per hour with an average cost of 20–30 US$/hectare (Gammoh and 
Oweis, 2011; Oweis, 2017).

relationship.outcome_raw: cost of building the micro-catchment bunds with the Vallerani plough: 20-30 US$ per hectare (about 3 ha per hour)

context.practice_as_described: Rangeland rehabilitation with Vallerani mechanised micro-catchment water harvesting (MWH): a tractor-pulled plough cuts intermittent contour bunds (pits about 3 m long, 2 m apart, 0.3-0.5 m deep with subsoiling to 0.7 m) that collect runoff and sediment from 10-17 m uncultivated interspace strips upslope; native saltbush (Atriplex halimus) seedlings were planted in the bunds in 2014 and grazing was excluded. Baseline: the untreated interspace (the runoff-contributing strip upslope of each bund), sampled within 2 m of the shrub - not land outside the scheme. The authors could not separate the effect of the water harvesting from that of the planted shrubs.
context.note: Soil samples 0-10 cm under 15 shrubs in 3 bunds vs the matching upslope interspaces, one date (21 February 2018, peak of the rainy season), four years after establishment; one-way ANOVA with shrub as random effect. Prior land use: grazing and barley cropping. Cited second-hand from Gammoh & Oweis 2011 and Oweis 2017. Covers mechanised bund construction only, not seedlings, planting or fencing. Currency year not stated.

units.question: Tatsumi 2021, reporting other studies, says a tractor plough builds runoff-catching bunds on about 3 ha an hour at US$20 to 30 per hectare. We recorded that cost. Looks right. Approve keeps it. Reject: building cost for small runoff basins still has no rating; confidence falls from medium to very low. AI's view: The cost range is in the quote.

context.practice_as_described: Rangeland rehabilitation with Vallerani mechanised micro-catchment water harvesting (MWH): a tractor-pulled plough cuts intermittent contour bunds (pits about 3 m long, 2 m apart, 0.3-0.5 m deep with subsoiling to 0.7 m) that collect runoff and sediment from 10-17 m uncultivated interspace strips upslope; native saltbush (Atriplex halimus) seedlings were planted in the bunds in 2014 and grazing was excluded. Baseline: the untreated interspace (the runoff-contributing strip upslope of each bund), sampled within 2 m of the shrub - not land outside the scheme. The authors could not separate the effect of the water harvesting from that of the planted shrubs.
context.note: Soil samples 0-10 cm under 15 shrubs in 3 bunds vs the matching upslope interspaces, one date (21 February 2018, peak of the rainy season), four years after establishment; one-way ANOVA with shrub as random effect. Prior land use: grazing and barley cropping. Table 1 (p4) 'Soil water content, pH, electrical conductivity (EC), organic matter content, and organic nitrogen (N) content ...': water content F = 197.1, P < 0.001. Single sampling date; the authors cite other work (p6) that bund soil moisture stays higher than the interspace through the year. Mechanism (p2): the bunds receive surface runoff from the upslope micro-catchment. Comparator is the runoff source area of the same system, which may be drier than unworked land.

units.question: Tatsumi 2021 measured soil moisture of 20.1% in the bunds vs 12.1% in the bare strips between them. We recorded a strong moisture gain. context.practice_as_described: Sand dams: small concrete (mortar and rock) walls 1-4 m high built by communities with the NGO SASOL across ephemeral (seasonal) riverbeds; sand accumulates behind the wall and stores rainy-season runoff as shallow groundwater in the sand, which protects it from evaporation and prolongs the period water can be abstracted from scoop holes (p6, p9). BASELINE (comparator): survey households without a dam (no dam built, or a dam that broke), and each household's own situation before dam construction / five years earlier (recall survey of 98 households with and 39 without dams, 2006; p6).
context.note: Section 1.2 SASOL (report p3 = PDF p9): programme figure reported by the implementing NGO, not measured by the survey; community labour is not costed. Elsewhere the report gives material costs 'around US$ 5000' per dam (PDF p10), 'less than EUR 30 per household' (summary, PDF p7) and 'US$ 35 per capita' (PDF p57) - inconsistent denominators. Each dam serves about 150 people in the dry season (PDF p9). Design: cross-sectional household survey with five-year recall, with-dam vs without-dam groups; dams not randomly placed; the authors check that rainfall does not explain the group differences (Table 4.1, p29) but households with dams also apply more terracing, bunds and grass lines (p30-31) and the effect of those cannot be separated (p31, p53).

units.question: Rockström 2009 says the two driest Kenyan sites had complete crop failures in most seasons, with zero maize at Machakos in a drought. We recorded this as in-field water capture (ripping and pits) giving no protection in drought. But the paper gives failure per site, not per treatment, and ripping alone is not counted as water harvesting. Approve keeps it. Reject: drought protection for in-field water capture on crop-livestock farms rises from moderate to very high; the highland and semi-arid lines would then differ from it and show separately. AI's view: The quote reports failure per site, so whether the pit treatments themselves failed needs a look at the paper's per-treatment results.

units.quote:
Si les crues ont été suffi-
samment nombreuses, mais pas trop fortes, cette portion de l’oued se trouve 
stabilisée suite au captage des sédiments transportés et aux travaux de consoli-
dation réalisés par les paysans : les pics des crues et les transports solides sont 
réduits, l’étiage stabilisé. (English: If the floods have been numerous enough but not too strong, this stretch of the wadi becomes stabilised through the capture of transported sediment and the consolidation work done by the farmers: flood peaks and sediment transport are reduced, low flow stabilised.)

relationship.outcome_raw: where floods were not too strong, the terraced stretch captures sediment and reduces flood peaks and sediment transport

context.practice_as_described: Low-terrace restoration in wadi beds: farmers build a stone wall to separate the low terrace from the active channel, then permeable stone lines or groynes (epis) and low bunds or tamarisk hedges inside, so that the plots capture part of the torrent floods, spread the sediment-laden water and pass the excess to the next plot; walls are raised as sediment accumulates; grass, then cereals and legumes, then fodder and fruit trees follow over about ten years (pp548-551). BASELINE: the unconsolidated wadi stretch (implied).
context.note: Chapter 40 (Roose, Sabir), "Restauration des basses terrasses devastees par les torrents dans le Haut Atlas (Maroc)", PDF pp548-554. Descriptive field observation. Paired with the asset unit: a sudden flood with a wall of water over two metres high devastates the works.

units.quote:
Grâce à des pièges à sédiments disposés dans 14 parcelles, DÍAZ et al. (2011) 
ont observé que l’épaisseur des sédiments déposés varie de 2 à 8 mm, soit en 
moyenne 46,1 t/ha/an. (English: Using sediment traps placed in 14 fields, DIAZ et al. (2011) observed that the thickness of deposited sediment ranges from 2 to 8 mm, i.e. on average 46.1 t/ha/yr.)

relationship.outcome_raw: gavia fields receive 2 to 8 mm of sediment a year, on average 46.1 t/ha/yr, eroded from the upslope catchment

context.practice_as_described: Gavias: macro-catchment runoff farming - runoff from a lightly grazed hillslope catchment (8 to 50 times the cropped area, 20-80 % slopes) is collected by drains and diversion channels into level fields of 600-10 000 m2 enclosed by earth walls 0.5-3 m high, each with an adjustable inlet and an overflow sill, often grouped in terrace cascades ("rosas"); about 7 300 ha; no irrigation and no fertiliser; cereals and legumes grown on the stored soil water (pp450-452). BASELINE: without the gavia walls the catchment sediment would pass downslope (implied).
context.note: Chapter 34 (Tejedor, Jimenez, Diaz), "Adaptations de l'agriculture a l'aridite dans les iles Canaries", PDF pp448-457. Cited secondary (Diaz et al. 2011, the chapter authors' group). Nutrient inputs with this sediment estimated (p453): 76.7 kg C and 8.7 kg N per mm of sediment per ha; 33.6 kg N/ha/yr; 35.3 kg total P/ha/yr; 48.8 kg K/ha/yr (not encoded).

l’utilisation 
d’impluvium en amont des parcelles pour le captage du ruissellement a permis 
de suppléer à l’insuffisance des pluies par un apport en eau de ruissellement 
estimé entre 150 et 180 mm. (English: the use of a runoff catchment (impluvium) upslope of the plots to capture runoff made up for the insufficient rainfall with a supply of runoff water estimated at between 150 and 180 mm.)

relationship.outcome_raw: the bare compacted runoff catchment supplied an estimated 150 to 180 mm of runoff water to the cropped strip

context.practice_as_described: IMPROVED SYSTEM (parcelle améliorée, Table 2 p630): stone lines (cordons empierrés, three levels of stones) every 20 m reinforced by a hedge of Atriplex nummularia / Medicago arborea, with the 10 m upslope of each line cultivated and the rest (230 m2) left bare and compacted as a runoff catchment (impluvium) feeding the cropped strip; contour subsoiling to 20 cm and harrowing; post-harvest mulch; selected wheat seed; herbicides and pesticides; organic and mineral fertiliser; biennial wheat/faba bean rotation under apricot trees; cypress and casuarina windbreaks (pp627-628). BASELINE (comparator): the regional control (témoin régional / traditionnel) - traditional wheat-grazed fallow, ploughed downslope 60-80 cm deep with a share plough, local seed, no fertiliser or pesticide. THIS UNIT: the bare, compacted 230 m2 impluvium upslope of each 10 m cropped strip (micro-catchment runoff farming).
context.note: Chapter 47 (Arabi, Bourougaa, Kedaid), "Lutte antierosive et intensification de l'agriculture en milieu steppique (Boughezoul, Algerie)", PDF pp626-634. Primary data: three contiguous 23 x 20 m (460 m2) runoff plots, 2000-2004, updated 2011 - one plot per treatment, no replication or statistical test (#57: unreplicated comparison, cap at moderate in synthesis). Estimated supply ("estimé"), not a measured soil-moisture difference; water added to the cropped strip against rain of 230-250 mm.

units.question: Roose 2017 (Algeria chapter) says the bare runoff catchment above each cropped strip supplied an estimated 150-180 mm of extra water. We recorded more soil moisture from small catchments. Looks right; it is an estimate from one plot. Approve keeps it. Reject: the separate agro-pastoral water shortage line (moderate positive, 2 papers) would no longer show, as it would then match the overall rating. AI's view: The 150-180 mm figure is in the quote and the catchment is named.

units.quote:
Même lors des années les 
plus sèches (p < 100 mm), le système des « gavias » permet de stocker près 
de 350 mm dans le mètre supérieur du profil, ce qui correspond à 
environ 150 mm d’eau disponible pour la culture. (English: Even in the driest years (p < 100 mm), the gavias system stores nearly 350 mm in the top metre of the profile, corresponding to about 150 mm of water available to the crop.)

relationship.outcome_raw: in the driest years (rain under 100 mm) gavia fields still store nearly 350 mm in the top metre, about 150 mm plant-available

context.practice_as_described: Gavias: macro-catchment runoff farming - runoff from a lightly grazed hillslope catchment (8 to 50 times the cropped area, 20-80 % slopes) is collected by drains and diversion channels into level fields of 600-10 000 m2 enclosed by earth walls 0.5-3 m high, each with an adjustable inlet and an overflow sill, often grouped in terrace cascades ("rosas"); about 7 300 ha; no irrigation and no fertiliser; cereals and legumes grown on the stored soil water (pp450-452). BASELINE: the same land under rain alone (under 100 mm in such years; implied).
context.note: Chapter 34 (Tejedor, Jimenez, Diaz), "Adaptations de l'agriculture a l'aridite dans les iles Canaries", PDF pp448-457. Uncited statement in the chapter (authors' own research group; Jimenez et al. 2002 cited nearby). The wheat yield is low and variable (mean 1.2 t/ha grain, p452) - no without-gavia comparison.

units.question: Roose 2017 (Canary Islands chapter) says even in the driest years (under 100 mm rain) gavia fields store nearly 350 mm in the top metre, about 150 mm usable by crops. We recorded more soil moisture. No without-gavia figure is given, but with under 100 mm rain the extra can only come from captured runoff. Approve keeps it. Reject: the separate high-income drought lines (low, 2 papers) would no longer show, as they would then match the overall rating; high-income water shortage stays strong positive but confidence falls from high to medium. AI's view: The 350 mm figure is in the quote and the comparison with rain alone follows from the numbers.

relationship.outcome_raw: potato yield (t per ha), terraced vs non-terraced fields, mean of the dry growing seasons (SPI-classified)

context.practice_as_described: Terrace and grassed waterway system on commercial potato fields in the Black Brook watershed, northern New Brunswick, Canada (built since the late 1980s): long, steep fields divided into shorter sections by soil berms built along the contour, discharging into grassed waterways, to cut erosion. Potato rotated with grain and forage. BASELINE (comparator): non-terraced potato fields in the same watershed over the same 20 years (48% of potato fields terraced, 52% not).
context.note: Yields: farm records 1992-2011 (observed, not modelled). Years classed by the Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI) of the growing season: 5 dry, 12 normal, 3 wet (p6, Fig. 4). Soil moisture was NOT measured: it was simulated with the Soil and Water Assessment Tool (SWAT) model, calibrated for streamflow and baseflow but not validated against measured soil moisture (p8). No significance test on the terraced-vs-nonterraced mean yields per climate class. High-income, temperate setting; transfer to smallholder terraces is weak. Mechanism (p8): berms break long slopes, slow runoff and lengthen infiltration time, raising soil moisture; in wet years the extra moisture depresses potato yields. Fig. 5 ('Observed and simulated (SWAT) average potato yields of terraced and nonterraced fields under different climate conditions from 1992 to 2011'); observed bars only (SWAT-simulated yields left out: the model was not calibrated for potato varieties). Dry years by the drought index SPI (1995, 1997, 2001, 2002, 2007); the authors call them 'dry conditions', not a named drought event, so severity unspecified. Normal-year reference present (ev_crop_yield_lian19_2).

units.question: A 2019 Canadian potato study found terraced fields yielded 32.76 t/ha against 32.39 t/ha in dry years, about 1% more, with no test of significance. We recorded a slight gain in drought. A 1% difference is better read as no clear difference; in wet years non-terraced fields did slightly better. Approve keeps it. Reject: the high-income drought lines (low, 2 papers) disappear; terraces on rainfed farms stay moderate, confidence falls from very high to high. AI's view: A 1% untested difference is recorded as a benefit; it may be better read as no clear difference.

context.practice_as_described: Terraces on farmers' cereal plots across Ethiopia (barley, maize, teff, sorghum, wheat), recorded in the nationally representative Ethiopian Socioeconomic Survey (ESS) 2015/16: horizontal man-made plots, in Ethiopia mostly built as level ditches with the soil thrown uphill to form an embankment (fanya juu) and also as stone bunds, largely built through government / NGO soil-conservation campaigns. BASELINE (comparator): unterraced plots matched 1:1 on 30 household, environment and plot covariates by propensity score matching (PSM); outcome = crop-cut grain yield per hectare. Contour bunds (ploughing and planting across the slope, no capture structure) were analysed separately in the paper and are NOT extracted here.
context.note: Quasi-experimental: nearest-neighbour propensity score matching (PSM), average treatment effect on the treated (ATT) divided by the mean cereal yield (1379 kg per ha, Fig. 2/3 captions) to give percentage changes. Final dataset 1388 households, 2611 plots. Significance: the paper prints thresholds, not exact P values ('*, ** and **** refer to the .1, .05 and .001 levels'); 'p = .05' is read as significant at the 5% level (**), 'p = .1' as not significant (catalogue #51). Mechanism (p2): terracing cuts overland flow connectivity, raises infiltration and soil moisture and conserves nutrients; the normal-year yield penalty is attributed to the cropping surface taken up by benches or stones (p5). The 2015/16 meher season followed a strong El Nino; the author describes it as 'one of the worst drought in decades' (p2). Drought exposure tercile 'high' by share of dry days in the plot's growing period (p3: low below 48%, 'moderate (48–66%)', high above 66%; CPC gauge rainfall at 0.5 degree matched to plot planting and harvest dates). Fig. 3a ('Percentages changes in yields per hectare for a) terraced plots given the % of dry days during crop growth length'). Hazard severity 'severe' from the author's description of the 2015 event; the high tercile is the most exposed third of plots. P = 0.1 is not significant at 5% (catalogue #51); the author marks it '*' (10% level). Normal-year reference present (low-exposure tercile in the same study).

relationship.outcome_raw: rise of the water level in village wells in Batodi, Niger, between 1994 and 2004, attributed by the authors to the runoff-harvesting works

context.practice_as_described: Soil and water conservation works ('aménagements de CES' - conservation des eaux et des sols) on degraded rainfed cereal land: runoff-harvesting structures - zaï (planting pits, 'tassa' in Hausa), demi-lunes (crescent-shaped micro-catchments), cordons pierreux (contour stone bunds), digues filtrantes (permeable rock dams) - which, per the report (p19), break the surface crust and slow runoff so rain infiltrates and more water is stored for crops, while fines and nutrients are trapped in the pits; farmers add organic manure (fumure organique) to treated fields alongside the structures (p19, p44). Batodi village (Illéla, Tahoua, Niger), fields treated since the 1990s. BASELINE: well level in 1994 (before/after, no control well).
context.note: Regional synthesis of the 'Etude Sahel' (CILSS/USAID-funded study of 20+ years of natural-resource-management investment in Burkina Faso, Mali, Niger and Senegal); the figures come from the national study teams' reports, which this report summarises, so units are coded cited_secondary with the national report named. p43; p41 gives the detail: well water at -18 m in 1994 (after good rain) and -4 m in November 2004 (after a very bad rainy season); villagers explained that since their fields were treated rain infiltrates better and surface runoff has much decreased (mechanism). The authors flag this as anecdotal ('beaucoup d'anecdotes', p41) and call for a proper study. Rainfall is not controlled for. No band rule for metres -> strength unspecified.

units.question: Botoni & Reij 2009 report that runoff-harvesting works raised village well water by about 14 m in Batodi, Niger, 1994-2004. We recorded more groundwater. Reject: catchment water yield for water harvesting stays 'conflicting evidence' but confidence falls from high to low; the rainfed-cropping line stays 'slight benefit' with confidence high to medium. AI's view: Number and attribution are in the quote; the weak design is noted.

context.practice_as_described: Zai (also tassa, towalen): planting pits 20-40 cm wide and 10-20 cm deep dug with a pick every 80-120 cm in staggered rows on crusted, degraded land at the start of the dry season, the earth thrown downslope as a crescent; the untilled surface (5-10 times the pit area) is the runoff catchment; one or two handfuls of dried manure powder (1-3 t/ha), manure, compost or ash with straw are buried in each pit before the rains, attracting termites; sorghum or millet sown in the pits (PDF p504). The preceding sentence: the pits capture a good part of the runoff (design figure about 48 mm per ha). BASELINE: the runoff would otherwise leave the crusted field (implied).

context.note: Narrative review (literature survey of ISI Web and grey literature; no systematic protocol, no weighting). Only the review's OWN pooled findings are extracted: the Fig. 2 regression of compiled grain yields against precipitation with vs without RWH (data in Appendix B, not in the cached file), the authors' Table 1 evaluation ('The impact of RWH practices on important landscape functions in African drylands. The data basis is evaluated by us concerning the number of publications ...'), and their concluding statements. Single-study findings it cites go to the cited-originals list. Pooled across in-situ, micro-catchment and terracing families, hence cross_family. Table 1, row 'Groundwater recharge' (mechanism: improved infiltration; impact '+'; data basis 'Fair'). Text p4: 'Very few direct field measurements of groundwater recharge are available'; the evidence is largely farmers stating that in situ RWH enhanced water availability. Weak basis - treat as indicative.
